title: Notification System
subtitle: Multi-channel notification architecture: APNs/FCM push, SMS, email, priority isolation, and rate-limit backpressure.
keyTakeaways: Isolate high-priority transactional alerts (two-factor OTPs, fraud warnings) from low-priority marketing blasts using dedicated Kafka topics and worker pools so a 20M-user campaign never delays a login code.

Third-party delivery providers (Apple APNs, Google FCM, Twilio, SendGrid) have variable latencies and strict rate limits: workers must decouple ingestion from dispatch using dead-letter queues and tiered retry topics with exponential backoff.

Guarantee at-least-once delivery without duplicate user alerts by enforcing an idempotencyKey at the API gateway and checking a short-lived Redis deduplication key immediately before dispatching to external providers.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A centralized Notification Platform ingests event notifications from internal microservices and dispatches them across mobile push, SMS, and email while respecting user preferences, rate limits, and quiet hours.
bullets: Functional: Deliver multi-channel notifications (Push via APNs/FCM, SMS via Twilio, Email via SendGrid/SES); support transactional and marketing classifications.
Functional: User preference management (opt-out of marketing, channel preference, time-zone aware quiet hours); deduplication of repeated events.
Non-Functional: High throughput (support 50 million notifications/day) with low latency for transactional events (OTP delivery p99 < 5 seconds).
Non-Functional: At-least-once delivery with near-zero duplicate alerts experienced by end users.
Out of Scope: WYSIWYG email template authoring tools, SMS conversation two-way replying, and user-to-user in-app chat.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Notification platforms handle a mix of steady transactional traffic and massive bursts during scheduled marketing campaigns.
bullets: Daily Volume: 50 million notifications per day (~600 notifications/second average).
Peak Blast Rate: Marketing flash sales generate bursts of up to 50,000 notifications/second.
Channel Breakdown: 65% Mobile Push (APNs/FCM), 25% Email, 10% SMS.
Payload Sizing: Average notification payload is ~1 KB of JSON. 50 million * 1 KB = 50 GB/day of message data.
Downstream Constraints: Twilio SMS accounts are throttled (e.g., 100-200 SMS/sec); SendGrid enforces account-level concurrency limits.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Capacity planning centers around message broker throughput, worker thread sizing, and protecting downstream vendor rate limits.
bullets: Kafka partition sizing: 50,000 peak msgs/sec with a target of ~1,000 msgs/sec per partition requires at least 50 partitions on the high-throughput marketing topic.

Worker fleet sizing: If an external APNs/FCM HTTP/2 call takes an average of 50ms, one worker thread handles 20 deliveries/second. Delivering 10,000 push/sec requires 500 concurrent worker threads (or non-blocking async event loops).
Redis deduplication storage: Storing 50 million notification keys for 24 hours (key: `notif:dedup:{userId}:{eventId}`, 40 bytes) requires ~2.5 GB of Redis RAM.

codeSnippet.title: Notification System Capacity Estimation Worksheet
codeSnippet.code:
================================================================================
                NOTIFICATION SYSTEM CAPACITY ESTIMATION SHEET
================================================================================
1. THROUGHPUT & QPS BY CHANNEL (1.25 Billion Notifications / Day)
   - Mobile Push (1B/day)       : Avg = 11,574 QPS   | Peak (5x) = ~58,000 QPS
   - Email (200M/day)           : Avg = 2,315 QPS    | Peak (5x) = ~11,600 QPS
   - SMS (50M/day)              : Avg = 579 QPS      | Peak (5x) = ~2,900 QPS
   - Total Dispatch QPS         : Avg = ~14,468 QPS  | Peak (5x) = ~72,500 QPS

2. REDIS CACHE MEMORY (RAM)
   - User Prefs & Device Tokens : 100M DAU * 500 Bytes       = 50 GB RAM
   - 24h Idempotency Keys       : 1.25B keys * 64 Bytes      = 80 GB RAM
   - Template Cache             : 5,000 templates * 50 KB    = 250 MB RAM
   - Total Redis Cluster RAM    : ~130 GB Primary (260 GB with 1x Replica)

3. 5-YEAR PERSISTENT STORAGE
   - Daily Notification Logs    : 1.25B/day * 500 Bytes      = 625 GB / day
   - 90-Day Hot Store (Cassandra, RF=3) : 625 GB * 90 * 3    = ~168.75 TB
   - 5-Year Raw Log Volume      : 625 GB/day * 365 * 5       = 1,140 TB (1.14 PB)
   - 5-Year S3 Archive (4:1 Zstd): 1,140 TB / 4              = ~285 TB

4. NETWORK BANDWIDTH (External Provider Egress)
   - Peak Push + SMS Egress     : 60,900 QPS * 1 KB          = 60.9 MB/sec
   - Peak Email Egress          : 11,600 QPS * 25 KB         = 290.0 MB/sec
   - Total Peak Egress          : ~351 MB/sec (2.81 Gbps)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: The ingestion API must accept notifications synchronously with minimal latency, returning an acknowledgment immediately while processing delivery asynchronously.
bullets: Ingestion API: `POST /v1/notifications/send` takes `{ recipientUserId, templateId, channel, priority: "HIGH"|"LOW", idempotencyKey, templateParams }` and returns `{ notificationId, status: "QUEUED" }`.
User Preferences Schema: PostgreSQL table storing user channel toggles, unsubscribed categories, and quiet-hour time windows.

Notification Log Schema: Cassandra or DynamoDB table partitioned by `(user_id, date)` recording delivery attempt timestamps, external provider message IDs, and terminal status (`DELIVERED`, `BOUNCED`, `FAILED`).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The architecture decouples ingress validation from rate-limited channel dispatchers using priority-tiered message queues.
bullets: Notification Ingestion Gateway: Validates payloads, checks client idempotency keys, and writes to Kafka topics.
Preference & Template Engine: Queries Redis (with DB fallback) to verify user opt-ins and formats personalized messages.
Priority Kafka Brokers: Separate topics for `notifications-high-priority` (OTPs, password resets) and `notifications-bulk` (promotions).
Channel Worker Fleets: Specialized consumer pools for APNs, FCM, SMS, and Email with built-in token-bucket rate limiters matching vendor quotas.
Vendor Feedback Webhooks: Receives asynchronous delivery receipts and bounce events from Twilio and SendGrid.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: A robust notification engine manages deduplication, vendor throttling, and transient failure recovery through tiered retry queues.
bullets: Deduplication flow: Before publishing to Kafka, the gateway sets `SET notif:dedup:{idempotencyKey} 1 NX EX 86400` in Redis. If the key exists, it returns the existing notification ID immediately without re-enqueuing.
Vendor rate-limit handling: If Twilio returns HTTP 429, the SMS worker pauses consumption on that partition and routes the batch to a delayed retry topic.

Tiered retry queues: Failed dispatches move through `retry-1m`, `retry-5m`, and `retry-15m` topics before moving to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) for operator inspection, preventing transient provider blips from dropping customer alerts.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Defensive architecture ensures that external vendor outages or database slowdowns do not disrupt critical notifications.
bullets: Vendor multi-homing: Maintain backup SMS and Email providers (e.g., Twilio primary with Infobip backup; SendGrid primary with AWS SES backup). If error rates exceed 5% on the primary, automatically shift traffic to the secondary.
Quiet-hour deferral: If a marketing notification is scheduled during a user's local night window (e.g., 10 PM to 8 AM), delay the message in a scheduled delivery queue until morning.
Preventing OTP starvation: High-priority transactional queues must have strictly dedicated worker instances that never scale down to zero and never pull from bulk marketing topics.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees zero latency degradation for critical 2FA OTPs during 50M-user marketing promotional spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires managing multiple worker pools and duplicate queue infrastructure.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Any platform sending both authentication/security alerts and commercial promotional emails.

tradeOffs.option: Single Unified Message Queue with Priority Header
tradeOffs.pros: Simpler infrastructure footprint; single consumer group to monitor and deploy.
tradeOffs.cons: Head-of-line blocking: a sudden surge of 10 million marketing messages can delay transactional alerts in queue.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Early-stage platforms with modest notification volumes (< 100k messages/day).

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees SMS deliverability through regional carrier outages and vendor billing account holds.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires maintaining multiple vendor contracts, SDK abstractions, and synchronization of delivery status webhooks.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Mission-critical enterprise platforms and international consumer apps operating across diverse telecommunications markets.

interviewTip: Always separate transactional notifications (OTPs, fraud alerts) from marketing blasts: explain that sharing the same queue leads to head-of-line blocking where a 10-million-user promotional email push delays a customer's 2FA login code by 15 minutes.
